## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- **Describe** a linear classifier as a separating hyperplane — a line or plane $w \cdot x + b = 0$
  whose side decides the class. *(Understand)*
- **Explain** the Perceptron learning rule and **analyze** its convergence: guaranteed on linearly
  separable data, never settling otherwise. *(Understand / Analyze)*
- **Contrast** the ways a linear classifier can pick its line (perceptron, logistic, SVM) and the
  multiclass strategies (one-vs-rest vs softmax). *(Analyze)*

  lessons develop. *(Analyze)*

## Why This Matters

L04 handed you *one* linear classifier — logistic regression. Step back and a pattern appears:
a logistic model, a perceptron, a support vector machine — every linear classifier ends
up drawing the **same kind of object**, a flat boundary that splits the feature space in two. This
lesson names that object, the **separating hyperplane**, and meets the *original* algorithm that
learns one from its mistakes: the **Perceptron** (Frank Rosenblatt, 1958). It matters twice over —
as the conceptual root of every later linear classifier, and as the single "neuron" that, stacked
into layers, becomes the neural networks of Unit V.

::: {.callout-tip title="Analogy"}
The Perceptron is a student who studies **only the problems they got wrong**. It checks each
example; if it is already right it does nothing, and if it is wrong it nudges the boundary a little
toward fixing that case. Repeat over the whole set, again and again — and *if a clean dividing line
exists*, this stubborn habit is guaranteed to find one.
:::

## The Separating Hyperplane

L04 ended on a key fact: logistic regression's decision boundary — the place where the label flips
— is the set of points with linear score zero, $w \cdot x + b = 0$, which is a straight line in two
features (a flat plane in three, a *hyperplane* in general). That object is the whole story of
linear classification:

- Compute a **score** $t = w \cdot x + b$ — a weighted sum of the features plus a bias.
- The **sign** of the score is the prediction: one class when $t \geq 0$, the other when $t < 0$.
- The boundary itself is where $t = 0$ — the separating hyperplane.

Every linear classifier in this course — the Perceptron here, logistic regression (L04), the SVM
(L08) — is *exactly this*: a choice of $w$ and $b$, i.e. a choice of hyperplane. What separates the
methods is **how they choose it**.

## The Perceptron Learning Rule

The Perceptron predicts with a hard **step** instead of a smooth sigmoid:

$$\hat{y} = \text{step}(w \cdot x + b) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } w \cdot x + b \geq 0 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

It learns by walking through the training points and reacting **only to its mistakes**. For each
point $(x, y)$ it predicts $\hat{y}$ and applies the update

$$w \leftarrow w + \eta\,(y - \hat{y})\,x, \qquad b \leftarrow b + \eta\,(y - \hat{y})$$

where $\eta$ is a small **learning rate**. Read the rule case by case and it is almost obvious:

- **Correct** ($y = \hat{y}$): the term $(y - \hat{y})$ is zero — no change.
- **Should have said 1, said 0** ($y - \hat{y} = +1$): add a multiple of $x$ to $w$, tilting the
  boundary *toward* calling this point positive next time.
- **Should have said 0, said 1** ($y - \hat{y} = -1$): subtract — tilt the other way.

Each mistake nudges the line a little in the direction that would fix *that* point. That is the
entire algorithm:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  X["next point (x, y)"] --> S["score t = w . x + b"]
  S --> P["predict y-hat = step(t)"]
  P --> C{"mistake?<br/>(y-hat != y)"}
  C -->|no| X
  C -->|yes| U["nudge the line:<br/>w += eta (y - y-hat) x<br/>b += eta (y - y-hat)"]
  U --> X
```

Note the contrast with L03 and L04: gradient descent minimizes a *smooth* loss (MSE, log loss) by
following its slope. The Perceptron has no smooth loss — it just corrects mistakes. That difference
is exactly what gives it its famous strength *and* its famous weakness.

## Convergence: Its Strength and Its Limit

The **Perceptron convergence theorem** says: if the two classes are **linearly separable** — some
hyperplane splits them perfectly — then the mistake-driven rule reaches zero training errors in a
*finite* number of passes. The lab watches this happen: the error count falls to zero and the
updates stop.

The flip side is just as important. If the classes are **not** linearly separable — they overlap,
so no single line can split them — the Perceptron **never settles**. There is always some
misclassified point demanding a nudge, so the boundary keeps moving forever; where you happen to
stop it is arbitrary. The lab shows this too: on overlapping data the error count bounces around
and never reaches zero.

::: {.callout-note title="Deep Dive: why separable data converges (Optional)" collapse="true"}

The classic proof bounds the number of updates by $(R/\gamma)^2$, where $R$ is the radius of the
data (how far the farthest point sits from the origin) and $\gamma$ is the **margin** (how wide the
gap is between the classes for the best separating hyperplane). Each mistake moves $w$ a controlled
amount *toward* a true separator while the squared length of $w$ can only grow so fast; the two
facts squeeze the update count to a finite number. A wider margin (bigger $\gamma$) means faster
convergence. The full derivation belongs to a learning-theory text; what you need here is the
consequence: **separable means finite; non-separable means forever.**
:::

## One Boundary, Many Ways to Choose It

On separable data the Perceptron finds *a* separating line — the first one its corrections land on.
But many lines separate the same data, and the Perceptron has no preference among them. Other linear
classifiers do, and that preference is what defines them:

| Method | How it picks the separating hyperplane | Where |
|--------|----------------------------------------|-------|
| **Perceptron** | any line that separates — it stops at the first one mistakes lead it to | this lesson |
| **Logistic regression** | the maximum-likelihood line — the one giving the best-calibrated probabilities | L04 |
| **Support vector machine** | the maximum-margin line — the one with the widest gap to the nearest points | L08 |

Same object, three different rules for choosing it. The lab makes the Perceptron's indifference
concrete: change the order it sees the points and it converges on a *different* perfect line.

## Multiclass: One-vs-Rest and Softmax

A single hyperplane splits *two* classes. For $K$ classes there are two standard moves:

- **One-vs-rest** — train $K$ separate binary classifiers ("class $k$ or not"), then for a new point
  pick the class whose classifier is most confident. scikit-learn's `Perceptron` does this
  automatically for more than two classes.
- **Softmax** — one model with one score per class, turned into probabilities that sum to 1 (L04).

One-vs-rest reuses any binary classifier as a black box; softmax is a single, jointly-trained model.
Both are in daily use; softmax is the one that reappears as the last layer of every classification
network in Unit V.

## Discriminative vs Generative: The Bridge to L06-L07

The Perceptron, logistic regression, and the SVM all answer the question *"which side of the
boundary is this point on?"* directly. They model $P(y \mid x)$ — or just the boundary — and never
ask what a class *looks like*. These are **discriminative** classifiers.

The next two lessons take the opposite route. **Generative** classifiers model each class
separately — what a typical example of class $k$ looks like, $P(x \mid y = k)$ — and then use Bayes'
rule to turn that around into a prediction.

| | Discriminative | Generative |
|--|----------------|------------|
| **Models** | the boundary / $P(y \mid x)$ directly | each class $P(x \mid y)$, then Bayes' rule |
| **Asks** | "which side of the line?" | "which class does this most look like?" |
| **Examples** | Perceptron, logistic regression, SVM | Gaussian discriminant analysis (**L06**), Naive Bayes (**L07**) |

Same goal — a label — reached from opposite directions. Keeping the distinction straight is what
makes the next two lessons click into place.

## When to Use / When NOT to Use

- **Use a linear classifier when:** the classes are roughly separable by a line/plane; you want a
  fast, interpretable model (one weight per feature); you need a strong baseline.
- **Avoid the bare Perceptron when:** you actually want probabilities (use logistic regression) or
  the single best-margin boundary (use the SVM); or when the data is not linearly separable, where
  it will never converge. In practice the Perceptron is taught for *understanding*, not deployed —
  but understanding it is the price of admission to neural networks (L14).

## Common Pitfalls

- **Expecting convergence on overlapping data.** If the classes are not linearly separable, the
  Perceptron loops forever; "more epochs" will not help. Cap the epochs and switch to a model built
  for overlap (logistic, SVM).
- **Reading a Perceptron line as *the* answer.** It found *a* separator, not the best one. A
  different point order gives a different line. When the specific boundary matters, use the SVM's
  max-margin choice (L08).
- **Confusing discriminative with generative.** A linear classifier draws a boundary; it does not
  describe the classes. "What does a typical class-1 example look like?" is a generative question
  (L06-L07), and a Perceptron cannot answer it.

## FAQ / Industry Reality

**"Is the Perceptron obsolete?"** — As a standalone classifier, mostly yes — logistic regression
and SVMs beat it on the jobs it was built for. But it is far from a museum piece: a single neuron in
a modern network *is* a perceptron with a smooth activation, and the whole of Unit V is built by
stacking and training them. Learn it here and the neural networks later are not a new idea, just a
deep one.

**"Perceptron or logistic regression?"** — Logistic, almost always: it gives probabilities, it
handles overlap gracefully, and it converges on a principled (max-likelihood) line rather than an
arbitrary one. The Perceptron's value is conceptual — the simplest thing that *learns* a linear
boundary, and the clearest place to see the mistake-driven idea.

**"Why does overlapping data never converge?"** — Because the rule only stops when there are zero
mistakes, and if no line can separate the classes, there is always at least one mistake left to
chase. It is not a bug or a bad learning rate — it is the theorem's contrapositive. Smooth-loss
models (logistic) and max-margin models (SVM) were designed precisely to do something sensible when
perfect separation is impossible.

## Summary / Cheat-sheet

| Concept | The one-liner |
|---------|---------------|
| Separating hyperplane | $w \cdot x + b = 0$; the sign of the score is the class |
| Linear classifier | a choice of hyperplane; methods differ in *how* they choose it |
| Perceptron rule | correct on mistakes only: $w \mathrel{+}= \eta(y - \hat{y})x$ |
| Convergence | separable means finite passes; non-separable means never settles |
| Pick-the-line | perceptron (any) · logistic (max-likelihood) · SVM (max-margin) |
| Multiclass | one-vs-rest ($K$ binary models) or softmax (one model) |
| Discriminative vs generative | learn the boundary $P(y\mid x)$ vs model each class $P(x\mid y)$ |
